data.title: Trump Doubles Down On Tariff Stupidity, Leans Nothing From Election
data.description:
My base case was Trump would act foolishly after the election, already proven.

Trump Turns to Section 301 Tariffs

The New York Times reports Trump Administration Unveils New Tariffs for Dozens of Countries, Citing Unfair Practices

The Trump administration proposed a slate of new tariffs on Wednesday targeting imports from dozens of countries, including China, Japan and the members of the European Union, marking the latest expansion of a global trade war that faces mounting obstacles in Congress and the courts.

The administration framed the duties as a response to unfair trade practices, as it accused some of its closest economic partners of overproducing certain products, undercutting American businesses and contributing to a swelling U.S. trade deficit.

The newly unveiled roster of tariffs included a 20 percent tax on some imports from China, which the Trump administration signaled it could ratchet up — to 40 percent — if Beijing does not hew to the terms of a trade truce it has struck with Washington.

The Trump administration also proposed similarly high and potentially escalating rates on goods from the 27 members of the European Union and other trading partners including Cambodia, India, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam. Some of those duties could reach up to 20 percent as well. And it coupled the sweeping action with a separate, specific proposal seeking to raise rates on Brazil, targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.

Before the new tariffs take effect, the administration must fulfill a set of final regulatory requirements, which would include seeking public feedback, according to Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative, who appeared Wednesday on CNBC. He described the approach as “targeted,” but noted that discussions continued with each of the affected trading partners.

In many cases, though, Mr. Greer said the tariffs would not stack on top of those that the administration had already put in place. That included duties that President Trump has applied on national security grounds to products such as steel and cars. He said the White House also sought to keep its tariffs in line with the trade agreements it had already brokered.

The battery of new tariffs nonetheless arrived at a precarious political moment for Mr. Trump, who has continued to engage in a strategy of aggressive trade brinkmanship even after the Supreme Court struck down his initial slate of country-by-country duties this year.

The announcement also appeared to rankle the country’s closest allies and trading partners. Some had already struck deals with Mr. Trump to avert higher tariffs — or were in the midst of negotiations — when the administration signaled Wednesday that it could raise rates even higher.

Mr. Trump’s newly proposed tariffs on the European Union would be set at 15 percent, as the agreement between trans-Atlantic partners had stipulated. But the administration also warned it could raise rates as high as 25 percent if it found compliance was “unsatisfactory.”

Terrible Time for New Tariffs

The Wall Street Journal reports Why This Is a Terrible Time for New Tariffs

Given their unpopularity, there is never a good time to raise tariffs. That said, this week was especially bad.

The Trump administration announced a new round of tariff increases Wednesday at the same time a key measure of inflation reached a three-year high—and mere weeks after Republicans were crushed in a midterm election that turned on affordability.

The tariffs will take effect after a comment period scheduled to end Jan. 5 and hearing scheduled for Jan. 25. The aggregate impact on inflation is likely to be modest; the U.S. Trade Representative said they incorporate, rather than stack on top of, existing duties and won’t exceed previously agreed caps in deals negotiated with trading partners like the European Union.

The Budget Lab at Yale University estimates the new levies would lift the average effective tariff for the U.S. from 11.4% to 13.9%, close to the rate that prevailed before the February Supreme Court ruling. The group, founded by former Biden administration economists, estimates they could raise consumer prices by 0.3%.

Fed governor Chris Waller earlier this month said firms will raise prices if they think consumers can handle it: “I heard it just last week talking to somebody, ‘Man, we put through 3% because we think we can get it.’ And that’s when you start having problems of trying to get inflation down.”

San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said, “Increasingly we’re hearing businesses say, ‘I’m at the end of my line. I’m going to have to pass some of these input costs through.’”

This simply proves how visceral and unshakable Trump’s attachment is to tariffs. He certainly isn’t doing it for the financial or political rewards.

Pall Over Thanksgiving

Bloomberg reports Trump’s Tariffs Cast New Pall Over Thanksgiving

The debates around the supper table this year offer little to relax about. The invincible stock market suddenly seems wobbly and the data center frenzy — a pillar of the current expansion — shows cracks. Washington is gripped with talk of AI fears, spy scandals, corruption probes and pardons.

Two distant wars grind on. Interest rates look to go higher just before Christmas.

And in perhaps the most curiously timed policy move in either of his administrations, President Donald Trump’s new tariffs announced yesterday would make imports more expensive.

Americans are closer to the beginning than the end of rising food costs. Prices are also surging for generators and toilet paper after a series of tech failures spooked the public into stockpiling survival items.

Tone Deaf Economic Illiterate

Trump is a tone deaf economic illiterate, to put things politely.

It is indisputable that tariffs raise prices and cost jobs. And the election speaks for itself, except to MAGA republicans who still salute their moron-in-chief.

Trump believes Republicans lost the election because he was not on the ballot. Instead, it was a blowout precisely because voters acted like Trump was on the ballot.

This went into my analysis predicting Democrats would win 60 Senate seats in 2028 along with a Trifecta, White House, Senate, and House.

My Base Case Right Now Is Democrats Will Win 60 Senate Seats in 2028

On November 21, 2026 I wrote My Base Case Right Now Is Democrats Will Win 60 Senate Seats in 2028

It’s a “savagely brutal map” for Republicans in 2028. Meanwhile, Trump is Trump.

My Six-Point Base Case

  • Trump will continue his economically illiterate tarffs.

  • Trump will continue his racist and economically illiterate deportations.

  • Stephen Miller will continue to run policy.

  • Inflation will not be under control.

  • The Fed will hike rates and cause a recession.

  • Trump will get the blame.

In short, I expect Trump will be Trump.

Also, we will be dealing with an AI bubble that is now bursting coupled with sustained inflation due to spending out of control (or a nasty recession that kills demand and the stock market).

OK, two years is a long time.

Yes, indeed.It’s long enough for Trump to make an even bigger mess than I suggested.

data.title: United States Dollar Index Weakens Below 104.00 As AI Concerns Simmer
data.description:
The US Dollar Index (DXY), an index of the value of the US Dollar (USD) measured against a basket of six world currencies, currently trades near 103.70 in the early European trading hours on Friday. The DXY declines as traders look to equity markets for clues on direction as doubts about the AI trade trigger heightened volatility.

The DXY remains choppy, as markets are concerned that a deeper AI slowdown could weigh on US growth. However, the potential downside for the index might be limited amid expectations for US Federal Reserve (Fed) policy tightening.

"All eyes are on whether the downtrend in AI-related stocks will turn around," said Mizuho analysts.

Hotter-than-expected US core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation in October, continued economic growth, and hawkish comments from Fed officials lift the USD against its rivals.

The Fed’s preferred gauge of inflation, the US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index, jumped 3.8% in October from the previous year, the US Bureau of Economic Analysis showed on Wednesday. Excluding food and energy, so-called core PCE rose 3.3% YoY in October, above the market consensus of 3.2%. 

Fed Governor Christopher Waller signaled that he could support a larger half-percentage-point move to curb inflation. Traders are now seeing a quarter-point interest rate hike on December 9 as a near certainty, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.

"The risk-reward of chasing further USD gains looks less attractive, but hawkish Fed risks should keep the dollar supported," said Sim Moh Siong, an FX strategist at OCBC in Singapore.

Dollar gains as tighter US financial conditions temper Fed hike path

Analysts at MUFG/BTMU highlight that the US Dollar "has continued to strengthen amidst the deepening sell-off in US stocks and pullback for US yields from year-to-date highs." They note that the latest bout of "weakness in the US equity market is taking place at a time when there is building evidence of strengthening cyclical growth momentum in the US," a combination that is "encouraging a stronger US dollar."

In MUFG/BTMU’s view, this "strengthening cyclical momentum is encouraging the Fed to raise rates further into restrictive territory in an attempt to dampen growth and ease upside inflation risks." At the same time, they caution that "the Fed will also be wary of the risk that a more sustained period of equity market weakness and tightening of financial conditions, including a stronger US dollar, would help to dampen the need for rate hikes."

MUFG/BTMU point out that "financial conditions have tightened sharply since the Fed indicated it is considering speeding up the pace of rate hikes in the coming months," a shift that "partly reflect[s] fears that the Fed could overtighten policy." This balance between robust cyclical momentum and rapidly tightening financial conditions is seen as central to the Dollar’s current support and to the Fed’s evolving policy calculus.

Williams flags more Fed work on inflation, keeping Dollar bulls alert

Fed’s Williams delivers a speech that is broadly consistent with the established baseline, with the FXS Speechtracker score holding at 6.2/10, exactly in line with the historical average. The emphasis that the U.S. central bank “still has work to do” to get inflation back to the 2% target, alongside projections of 3.5% inflation in 2026 and a return to 2% only by 2028, underscores a still-hawkish bias despite acknowledging stable jobs and a resilient economy. While Williams notes that inflation pressures are not broadening much, the characterization of inflation as “still too high” with upside risks keeps the policy narrative tilted toward further restraint rather than imminent easing, a backdrop that tends to support the Dollar on balance.

The FXS Fed Sentiment Index rose by 0.35 points to 152.49, reinforcing that the overall policy tone remains firmly in hawkish territory well above the neutral 100 threshold. This incremental uptick, aligned with the steady 6.2/10 FXS Speechtracker score, signals that markets should continue to price a relatively restrictive Fed stance, with limited scope for near-term dovish surprises.

Technical Analysis: US Dollar Index retains a positive view in the near term

In the daily chart, Dollar Index Spot trades at 103.70. The near-term bias is bullish as price holds above the 100-day simple moving average (SMA) at 101.09 and the Bollinger Bands’ middle band at roughly 103.03, reinforcing an underlying bid after the recent breakout. The Relative Strength Index (14) at 61.36 stays in positive territory without being overbought, suggesting constructive momentum that could keep the index supported on dips.

On the downside, initial support is seen at the Bollinger middle band near 103.03, ahead of a broader demand zone defined by the lower Bollinger band at around 101.19 and the 100-day SMA at 101.09. On the topside, the Bollinger upper band at 104.87 acts as the next resistance, and a sustained move above this barrier would open the way for an extension of the current advance.

data.title: Oil: The Market Has Already Written Off The Energy Crisis
data.description:
As investors turn their attention back to technology stocks, the market seems to believe that the oil crisis is now behind us. The spectacular drop in prices since October has helped reassure financial markets, which are anticipating a normalization of supply conditions and a retreat in inflationary pressures.

This complacency is dangerous. Behind the decline in paper oil prices, the fundamentals of the physical market continue to deteriorate. Inventories are falling, flows through the Strait of Hormuz are contracting again, and the structure of futures contracts points to mounting pressure on near-term supply.

From a technical perspective, WTI crude has been trading within a broad contracting triangle since March. The recent correction has formed a bullish harmonic pattern known as a Bullish Bat, whose completion point D coincides with the triangle’s lower boundary, around $80. Although the Fibonacci ratios do not perfectly match those of a textbook pattern, this convergence of technical support levels strengthens the likelihood of a rebound. The chart target for this move lies at the triangle’s upper boundary, in a zone between $98 and $102 per barrel. This bullish scenario remains valid as long as the ascending trendline support holds.

Inventories falling out of season

At this time of year, crude oil inventories normally tend to build as demand slows seasonally.

Yet the latest US statistics paint a very different picture. Total petroleum stocks fell by 5.3 million barrels in one week, despite another 2.9 million-barrel drawdown from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR):

Commercial crude inventories did increase by 1.1 million barrels, but total commercial stocks of petroleum and refined products fell by 2.4 million barrels.

US strategic reserves now contain just 273.5 million barrels.

The oil surplus that financial markets regularly talk about fails to materialize in the inventory data.

Hormuz: flows deteriorate again

The situation in the Strait of Hormuz is deteriorating once more.

Oil flows through the strait have fallen back to around 6 million barrels per day on a seven-day average, compared with 20 million before the conflict:

More concerning still, a substantial gap is emerging between volumes loaded inside the Persian Gulf and those that actually make it through the strait.

Oil loadings in the Persian Gulf are running at nearly 16 million barrels per day, yet only 6 million barrels are currently passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

This gap suggests that oil is accumulating inside the Gulf, although the latest shipping data are preliminary and transit times need to be taken into account.

The market now appears convinced that Iran lacks both the means and the willingness to escalate the conflict. The absence of escalation around the Fujairah and Sohar transshipment hubs reinforces this view among traders.

But no one really knows Iran’s strategy – or its timeline.

The current status quo appears difficult to sustain. Any further escalation before year-end would come as political pressure on Donald Trump intensifies and oil reserve levels constrain the US room for maneuver.

The futures market is sending a warning signal

While oil prices have undergone a sharp correction, the spread between the first two Brent futures contracts has surged back to $3.82:

In practical terms, oil for delivery in January 2027 is trading $3.82 higher than oil for delivery in February.

This structure, known as backwardation, reflects a premium for immediate access to oil.

In a genuinely oversupplied market, one would expect the opposite. Traders would be incentivized to store oil and sell it later at a higher price.

Today, the market is instead rewarding prompt availability of barrels.

The spectacular decline in paper oil prices therefore masks persistent tightness in the front end of the curve.

Falling oil prices will not rescue the Fed

The compression of paper oil prices has an obvious political benefit: lowering inflation expectations and reassuring bond markets.

But the latest US inflation figures show the limits of this strategy.

The PCE index, the inflation gauge preferred by the Federal Reserve, continues to climb:

In October, US inflation measured by the PCE index reached 3.8% year-on-year, while core inflation, excluding energy and food, stood at 3.3% – well above the Fed’s 2% target.

Despite easing energy prices, underlying inflationary pressures are intensifying. US third-quarter growth has also just been revised up to 4.3% annualized.

Under these circumstances, the Fed is likely to raise rates in December. Markets are also anticipating another hike in January.

What happens if oil prices rise again while the Fed is already being forced to tighten monetary policy?

It’s not 2020 – but possibly 2022

Investors still seem to be thinking in terms of the 2020 scenario, when the collapse in financial markets triggered a historic drop in oil demand.

The current situation is radically different.

The main risk is not a collapse in demand, but a contraction in supply. In this respect, the comparison with 2022 seems far more relevant: equity markets can suffer sharp corrections while energy prices continue to rise.

Oil could therefore decouple from other financial assets during the next waves of equity-market liquidation.

If flows through Hormuz do not recover quickly, current prices could represent one of the last opportunities to buy a barrel below $100. In a scenario of prolonged shortages, that level could even become a floor in 2027.

The market has stopped paying attention to oil precisely when it should be watching it most closely.

The combination of another energy shock, persistent inflation and rising rates is likely to be one of the most underestimated risks facing financial markets as 2027 approaches.

Gold and the risk of another inflation shock

In the short term, the prospect of further Fed tightening and liquidity pressures could continue to weigh on gold prices. Over the medium term, however, another oil shock would confront central banks with a formidable dilemma: fighting inflation at the risk of triggering a financial crisis amid widespread excessive debt. Unlike in 2022, governments now have even less fiscal room to maneuver. Higher interest rates would substantially increase debt-servicing costs, while rising energy prices would undermine the real economy. It is precisely this monetary and fiscal predicament that reinforces gold’s appeal as a long-term protective asset.

data.title: Gold Declines To Near $3,550 Amid Hawkish Fed Expectations

"Spot gold is testing support around the mid-$3,000 region. "Bullion bulls are set to be kept on the back foot... But fresh risk-off events across global financial markets may support the precious metal, adding to persistent purchases from central banks,” Han added.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump prepared to raise tariffs on China, the European Union (EU), Mexico, Japan and dozens of other countries that Trump argues are harming American companies by supporting their own domestic industrial production, per the Wall Street Journal. Any signs of renewed trade tensions could boost safe-haven flows, benefiting the yellow metal in the near term.

Precious metals whipsaw as copper grinds to new lows

Analysts at Deutsche Bank highlight that “another asset class that saw some big moves over the last 24 hours were precious metals,” with price action turning notably volatile. By contrast, the bank reports that “industrial metals did lose further ground, with copper (-0.61%) down to its lowest since December 2025,” extending the recent weakness in base metals.

The emphasis that the U.S. central bank “still has work to do” to bring inflation back to the 2% target, alongside projections of 3.5% inflation at end-2026 and a return to 2% only by 2028, underscores a prolonged restrictive bias even as the economy is described as strong, resilient and supported by a stable job market. Upside inflation risks, uncertainty around energy prices and AI, and a 2.75% growth outlook for 2026–2027 collectively point to a Fed that is not yet ready to pivot, a backdrop typically supportive of the Dollar on rate expectations.

The FXS Fed Sentiment Index rises by 0.35 points to 152.49, reinforcing that the overall policy tone remains deep in hawkish territory. The combination of an unchanged FXS Speechtracker score and a higher FXS Fed Sentiment Index level suggests that markets see Williams’ remarks as confirming entrenched hawkishness rather than introducing a new dovish tilt, a configuration that should keep Dollar bulls comfortable with the current Fed narrative.

data.title: Rates Spark: Rates Resist Bearish Pressure As France Faces Rating Risk
data.description:
Bearish dynamics remain contained in European rates despite the ECB’s tightening bias and firmer energy prices. French spreads tightened ahead of S&P’s review, but political uncertainty and budget risks could warrant a negative outlook – and keep investors cautious

Bearish dynamics remain contained

Left on their own with the US out on holiday, European rates briefly tested the upside. While the European Central Bank accounts clearly pointed to the ECB’s tightening bias – maybe even beyond December – and energy prices also sneaked higher as tensions in the Middle East continue to simmer, a bearish dynamic failed to take hold in the end. What lingers is the uncertainty around the tech narrative.

S&P scheduled to review France after Friday’s market close

French bond spreads did manage to tighten over the past session, taking the 10y spread over Bunds below the 150bp threshold.

This seems to defy the risk of S&P lowering the outlook on the stable A+ rating it currently still attaches to France. Given the uncertain political backdrop, further budget slippage over the year and an eroding growth outlook, S&P may have enough reason to do just that. At the same time, it would no longer really come as a surprise. Fitch lowered the outlook of its A+ rating to negative at the end of October in an unscheduled move after having only just reviewed the country in August.

Moreover, markets are already pricing France more like a BBB-rated country. To be fair, much of this is likely an overshoot. In its recent Financial Stability Review, the ECB pointed to the procyclical role of hedge funds in eurozone government bond spread dynamics. At the same time, the lingering threat of a downgrade might create another hurdle for investors looking to return to the French bond market.

Replacing hedge fund demand may come at a costs to gilts

The Bank of England has reiterated its intention to introduce measures to strengthen the gilt repo market, which could negatively impact demand for gilts. Hedge funds have acted as an important marginal buyer over the past year, helping absorb the significant increase in gilt supply. A popular strategy is buying cash gilts and offsetting these positions with shorts in gilt futures, whereby repo markets offer the ability to leverage up such trades. The slight pricing difference between cash gilts and gilt futures can provide attractive returns. But if the repo costs were to rise, the attractiveness of such trades could fall.

In effect, hedge funds offer balance sheet capacity to house gilts, and therefore any headwinds to such trades can add upward pressure to gilt yields. But the impact is more nuanced. Because the gilt positions are hedged through futures, any unwind of the hedge fund positions should be relatively neutral in terms of term premium. We would, however, expect gilts to underperform swaps. The spread between swaps and gilts is strongly linked to the balance sheet costs of holding bonds. If hedge funds decide a trade is no longer attractive due to higher trading costs, then other players with higher balance sheet costs (such as banks) would have to jump in.

Friday's events and market view

We will see preliminary inflation data for November in France and Spain, where headline rates are expected to ease somewhat but remain at elevated levels. The ECB will also publish its consumer survey on expected inflation. ECB officials scheduled to speak are Chief Economist Philip Lane, Vice President Boris Vujčić, Germany's Joachim Nagel and France's Emmanuel Moulin.

In primary markets, Italy will auction 5y and 10y BTPS as well as 8y and 9y CCTeu floaters (in total up to 8bn).

data.title: Gold At Record Highs Is Not An Inflation Story. It Is A Trust Story.
data.description:
For three years running, central banks have bought more than 1,000 tonnes of gold annually, according to the World Gold Council. That is roughly double the average pace of the 2010s, and it has continued through rate cuts, rate hikes, a strong dollar and a weak one. When the official sector buys that consistently, retail sentiment stops being the driver. Something structural is underneath.

The standard explanation is inflation. It does not fit. Inflation in the major economies has fallen sharply from its 2022 peak, yet gold kept making record highs. Real yields, the old enemy of gold, stayed positive and high by historical standards, and gold rallied anyway. The correlations that governed the metal for two decades have broken, one after another.

What changed in 2022 was not consumer prices. It was the weaponization of reserves. When roughly $300 billion of Russian central bank assets were frozen, every reserve manager in the world learned the same lesson: a reserve asset is only yours if the issuer lets you keep it. Treasuries are safe in a market sense. They are not safe in a political sense. Gold has no issuer. That single property, irrelevant for forty years, is now being priced.

Look at who is buying. The National Bank of Poland, the People's Bank of China, the central banks of India, Turkey, and a rotating cast of emerging markets. These are not momentum traders. They are institutions with thirty-year horizons, and they are swapping paper claims on other governments for metal in their own vaults. The share of the dollar in disclosed global reserves has slid from above 70 percent at the turn of the century to the high 50s, per IMF COFER data (data.imf.org). Nobody is dumping dollars. They are simply hedging the system that produced them.

There is a second engine: debt. US federal debt is above $36 trillion and rising by roughly $2 trillion a year, with interest costs now rivaling the defense budget. Japan, Britain and France have their own versions. Bond markets can absorb a lot, but the question has shifted from "will these debts be repaid" to "in what currency, worth how much." Gold is the asset that asks that question loudest.

What does this mean for the price? Official-sector demand does not chase. It accumulates on weakness and ignores strength, which builds a floor under corrections. As long as reserve diversification continues, dips get bought by someone with deeper pockets and a longer clock than any hedge fund.

The risks to the view are real. A genuine peace dividend, a credible sanctions rollback, or a long stretch of high real yields with a calm geopolitical map would slow official buying. Gold also pays nothing, and when the premium for safety shrinks, opportunity cost returns. Watch the quarterly central bank demand data more than the daily fix; that is the tell.

But the bigger point stands. Gold is not signaling that your groceries will cost more next year. It is signaling that the plumbing of the international monetary system is being rebuilt with more redundancy and less trust. Investors who treat the rally as a bubble are fighting the one class of buyer that never has to sell.

This is analysis, not investment advice. Do your own research.

data.title: HPE Plunges Despite Raising The Bar For 2027
data.description:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise delivered exactly what the bulls were looking for after a punishing month for AI hardware: a clean beat, an above-the-range quarter, and a fiscal 2027 outlook that blew past where analysts had been modeling.

The stock's reaction was more complicated. Shares rallied 17% during Monday's regular session as technology stocks surged, then gave back all of the gain – and then some – to drop below $40 per share in early Wednesday trading.

A Beat on Every Line That Matters

Adjusted earnings came in at $1.43 per share, topping the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.29 by nearly 11% and clearing the top of management's own $1.20 to $1.30 range. That compares with $0.62 a year ago. Revenue rose 50% to $14.55 billion, edging past consensus, and HPE has now topped the Zacks consensus on earnings in each of the last four quarters.

Fiscal 2026 as a whole was transformational. Revenue grew 36% to $46.7 billion, adjusted earnings reached $3.97 per share, and free cash flow climbed to $4.5 billion from less than $1 billion the year before. Antonio Neri described HPE as "a fundamentally different company, with greater earnings power," and the numbers certainly back up the corporate language.

The Guidance Is the Story

The fourth quarter was good. The fiscal 2027 outlook was something else entirely. In September, management laid out a framework calling for revenue growth of 13% to 17% and earnings growth of 16% to 20%. On Monday evening, the company raised revenue growth to 27% to 35%, or $59.4 billion to $63.1 billion, and set adjusted EPS at $5.05 to $5.35.

Put those numbers next to the Street. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for fiscal 2027 stood at $4.74 per share on $55.12 billion in revenue, so the low end of the new range sits about 6.5% above consensus and the midpoint nearly 10% above it. First-quarter guidance of $1.30 to $1.40 compares with a consensus of $1.10. The midpoint of the annual range implies growth of about 31% on top of a year in which earnings nearly doubled.

Expect estimate revisions to move sharply higher over the next week, which is precisely the dynamic the Zacks Rank rewards; HPE (HPE - Free Report) entered the report as a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy).

Servers Carried the Quarter

Server revenue nearly doubled, up 94.7% to $8.8 billion, as the hyperscaler inferencing deal and the AI systems backlog converted to shipments. By my arithmetic, servers accounted for close to 90% of the company's year-over-year revenue increase and roughly 60% of total revenue.

Networking, the segment management has been touting, grew a more modest 12.3% to $3.1 billion, toward the top of management's 11% to 13% guide. Security slipped 1.8%. Networking operating margin eased to 22.1% from 23.4% a year ago.

The forward indicators were stronger: networking orders more than doubled, and networks-for-AI orders hit a record $1.2 billion in the quarter, with Neri putting the fiscal-year total in the "mid-$2 billion" range, inside the target he set. For fiscal 2027, management is targeting $7.5 billion to $8 billion of cumulative networks-for-AI orders, weighted to the back half as AMD Helios and Oracle deployments ramp.

None of that is a problem. But the segment outlook management gave on the call confirms that the 2027 upgrade leans more heavily on AI compute than on the Juniper pivot: Cloud & AI revenue is guided to grow 30% to 40%, against high-teens to low-20s growth for networking. Server demand is the more cyclical of the two.

Margins Held Up Better Than Feared

The margin picture is a quiet win. Non-GAAP gross margin stepped down to 38.2% from a record 40.4% in the third quarter, which was expected given the size and mix of the hyperscaler shipments, but it was still up 180 basis points from a year ago. More telling, Cloud & AI operating margin reached 18.4%, double the 9.3% of a year earlier and well above the mid-teens rate management had flagged.

The catch came on the call. Management guided Cloud & AI operating margin to about 14% for fiscal 2027, well below the 18.4% just reported, and said gross margin should moderate as the year progresses, driven by mix and the timing of large AI systems ramps. Marie Myers was candid: "we do expect to see some pressure in pricing."

Why the Stock Slipped

The post-release slide has a clearer explanation. The 17% Monday-session rally front-ran much of the good news, and the call then introduced two less comfortable details.


Image Source: StockCharts

The first is the margin step-down described above. The second came from a J.P. Morgan question: spread evenly, the fiscal 2027 networks-for-AI order target implies roughly flat quarterly orders versus the $1.2 billion just booked.

Management pointed to scale-out, scale-across and Helios networking trays as upside, but the arithmetic is fair. Neither undermines the guidance, but both temper how far investors should extrapolate one blockbuster quarter.

Bottom Line

At under $40, HPE trades at less than nine times the midpoint of its fiscal 2027 earnings guidance, a multiple that still prices in a great deal of skepticism.

Neri made the point himself on the call: "I don't see us at a multiple that is 8x-9x." The concentration in servers and the coming margin moderation are legitimate reasons for some caution. But a record $10.5 billion AI backlog, orders up 88%, a guide well above consensus and rising cash returns, all at a single-digit multiple, is not a stock I would be selling into this week’s downturn.

data.title: These 3 Retail Stocks Are Best Positioned To Benefit From Thanksgiving In 2026

The Thanksgiving shopping rush looks a little smaller this year.

The National Retail Federation estimates 182.7 million consumers plan to shop between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, down from 186.9 million last year.

With more consumers starting early, the retailers best positioned to benefit are the ones giving shoppers several reasons to spend across the weekend.

Walmart can turn a grocery trip into a gift purchase, Target is using exclusives to bring people into stores, and Amazon (AMZN) is putting deals inside a football broadcast.

Walmart can turn a $35 dinner into a bigger shopping basket

Walmart (WMT) advertised a 26-item Thanksgiving meal basket for $35 that serves 10. At $3.5 a person, the offer gives households a concrete reason to choose it for one of November’s biggest grocery trips.

The payoff can come from what shoppers add to the order, from roasting pans and extra desserts to toys they were already planning to buy.

Walmart’s main Black Friday sale went online Nov. 23, overlapping with the final days of Thanksgiving prep.

In-store deals begin Friday morning. That timing matters because Walmart’s US e-commerce sales rose 23% in its latest quarter.

A customer who orders groceries online can browse holiday deals in the same place, giving Walmart another chance to win the gift purchase before that shopper opens a rival’s app.

Target gives Black Friday shoppers a reason to show up

Target (TGT) has $30 Thanksgiving meal for six but the bigger opportunity comes Friday morning. The first 100 eligible shoppers at each store get a gift card, with one card per location worth $1,000.

Target is also rolling out exclusive Pokémon and Topps trading-card products. A giveaway can get people through the door. An exclusive gives them something to buy that they can’t easily price-check at a rival.

Target enters the weekend with store comparable sales up 4.6% in its latest quarter.

The question for investors is how much of that traffic turns into a fuller cart. A shopper who comes for a collectible and leaves with holiday décor, wrapping paper or another gift makes the promotion more valuable than the giveaway alone would suggest.

Amazon brings the sale to the football audience

Amazon’s (AMZN) holiday sale runs through Nov. 30, with two rounds of featured deals on both Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Its most distinctive sales pitch comes during Friday’s Pittsburgh Steelers–Denver Broncos game on Prime Video.

Viewers can use their remote or the Amazon Shopping app to see featured deals and buy merchandise during the broadcast, giving Amazon a chance to reach people who tuned in for football and may never have planned to browse a sale.

That extra attention has value beyond the items Amazon sells directly. Independent merchants can pay Amazon for services such as fulfillment, and brands can pay for ad placements.

For investors, that means a busy shopping weekend can generate revenue for Amazon even when another merchant makes the sale.

data.title: When A Stock Falls, Is The Business Really In Trouble?
data.description:
When a stock falls, has the business weakened or has the price come back in line with earnings? Chuck Carnevale uses FAST Graphs to show how earnings growth, cash flow, and the price you pay can shape long-term returns.

When a Stock Falls, Is the Business Really in Trouble?

A falling stock price tells you what investors are willing to pay today. To understand what the business is worth, look at what it earns, how much cash it generates, and what you can reasonably expect it to earn in the future.

In this FAST Graphs video, Chuck Carnevale demonstrates a simple way to start. He takes the stock price off the chart and looks at how the business performed on its own. Then he puts the price back on the chart to see where it tracked earnings and where it pulled away. It’s a practical application of a theme from All Investing Is Value Investing, the book Chuck co-authored with Professor Nathan Mauck.

A strong business can still be an expensive stock

Oracle (ORCL) and Amgen (AMGN) both grew earnings through difficult economic periods. Yet the returns Chuck shows vary widely depending on what an investor paid. In one Amgen example, buying at a lower valuation produced a higher annualized return than buying at a premium during a period of faster earnings growth. The starting price mattered enough to outweigh the difference in growth.

Alphabet (GOOGL) illustrates another point. Change the time frame on a FAST Graphs chart and the historical earnings growth rate can change with it. That can shift the valuation reference. Comparing several periods helps you see whether a particular growth rate reflects a sustained record or an unusually strong stretch.

Do the numbers support the business story?

Copart (CPRT) offers a concrete example of a competitive advantage. Its salvage yards and insurer relationships bring vehicles to auction, and a global network of buyers makes those auctions more valuable to insurers. Each side helps attract the other. That explains why the business has been hard to replicate. The valuation question is how much to pay for that advantage if future earnings grow more slowly than they did in the past.

Chuck asks a similar question about NVIDIA (NVDA). Using Ask Charles, he looks at how NVIDIA’s CUDA software ecosystem supports its competitive position and what the company’s balance sheet and cash generation say about the business. The valuation still depends on whether NVIDIA can deliver the earnings growth investors expect.

What does it take to recover from a 50% loss?

data.title: Fed Rate-Hike Bets Deliver Fresh Blow To Your Holiday Budget
data.description:
American households are getting squeezed from all sides this holiday season as stubborn inflation and a stronger-than-expected U.S. economy collide with a fresh wave of proposed tariffs.

For America’s consumers and borrowers, their money worries are no longer just a single interest-rate hike in December but perhaps a relentless tightening cycle that could push the Federal Reserve to keep raising the benchmark federal funds rate through January, March, and possibly beyond before rate cuts could resume in 2028.

“Additional tariffs complicate the inflation situation along with the lingering ways in which supply chains have been roiled due to the AI buildout, KPMG Chief Economist and Managing Director Diane Swonk said in a blog post. “The Fed is in a tough spot in December, weighing another rate hike but concerned about the speed with which a larger market correction could ripple through the economy.”  

Fresh economic PCE readings of hot, sticky, and broadening inflation in October and revised, sharply higher third-quarter GDP at 4.3% — the fastest pace since late 2023 — released Nov. 25 give central bankers ample reasons to lean hawkish with a 25-basis-point rate hike at the Federal Open Market Committee Dec. 8-9.

Minutes after those headlines crossed, the Trump administration unveiled proposed new tariffs targeting 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan, and the European Union, to counter what the administration calls foreign “excess industrial capacity.”

Truist Advisory Services Head of U.S. Economics Mike Skordeles said the year-over-year increase of headline and core PCE and the revised GDP report further confirm “for us that the Fed will deliver a quarter-point hike in December.’’ 

Skordeles said in an exclusive email to TheStreet that the proposed tariffs won’t be enacted until January at the earliest and won’t affect specific industries with national security-related levies, such as steel, aluminum and automobiles.

“The combination of the factors should limit the near-term implications, especially for most consumers,” Skordeles said. 

Persistent inflation puts Fed rate hikes in focus

The FOMC held rates steady in October at 3.75-4.0% after a 25-basis-point hike in September, amid sticky inflation from tariffs, the Iran War energy shock, and the AI demand-supply dynamic. It was the Fed’s first rate move of the year.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh vowed before and after taking over the role in May that the price stability side of its dual mandate is the independent central bank’s top commitment now that the labor market has stabilized from its 2025 softness.

Four Fed governors — Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, Michael Barr, Lisa Cook and Christopher Waller — and several regional bank presidents recently signaled decidedly hawkish tones, expressing that further policy tightening was necessary to bring inflation back to its 2% target, which it has missed for nearly six years. 

The Fed made three 25-basis-point cuts at its last three meetings of 2025 due to concerns about the labor market side of its mandate. Those insurance cuts need to be reversed as inflation data shows higher prices not only in energy costs but broadening into other sectors including services, the Fed’s hawks say.

So do some Fed watchers. Wall Street banks, including giants J.P. Morgan, Bank of America and Deutsche Bank, are also calling for a 25-basis-point hike in December plus additional 25-basis-point increases in January and March.

TheStreet

Traders price in Fed rate hikes into 2027  

According to the CME Group FedWatch Tool, following the latest inflation readings, futures traders see roughly a 97% to 98% probability of a 25-point-rate hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting.

But it probably won’t be a “one-and-done” deal.

CME FedWatch probabilities for the January FOMC meeting point to a strong chance of additional tightening, including a roughly 40.7% probability of another 25-basis-point hike and a 58.4% chance of a cumulative 50-basis-point increase. Markets also price in an additional rate increase in March if policymakers are unable to cool demand.

President Donald Trump and his allies have repeatedly called for lower interest rates of 1% or less for years, with the president blasting the Fed’s most recent actions as political retribution.

Trump has said the lower rates will help the depressed U.S. housing market plus reduce the interest the government pays on its $40.71 trillion debt.  

New tariffs aim to boost, balance American trade

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer’s office unveiled the proposals following an eight-month investigation into foreign industrial overcapacity and set the maximum potential tariff rates of 20% to 40%.

Separately, the administration proposed a new 10% tariff on finished commercial aircraft from Brazil and higher duties on over-quota Brazilian sugar after talks with the South American nation stalled.

The new tariff push, while not viewed as sweeping as April’s Liberation Day announcement, lands just three weeks after midterm elections reflected voter frustration over higher costs of living and skepticism about Wall Street, where volatility has been fueled by AI and other tech jitters. 

Dean Lyulkin, the CEO of Cardiff, a San Diego-based small business lender, said the Trump administration’s proposed tariffs fall mainly on Vietnam and Southeast Asia, and mostly on furniture, clothing, and other consumer goods.

“Even there, the additional tariff applies to the wholesale import value, not the retail price, and amounts to just 5% to 10% more,’’ Lyulkin said in an exclusive email to TheStreet.

Critics warn that new import levies amount to a tax on consumers and risk triggering another round of price increases that could force the Fed to keep interest rates higher for longer.

“There is zero reason for anyone, including investors and small business owners, to panic,’’ Lyulkin said. “If this headline is used to explain the market correction happening now, or to suggest it adds new risks to the U.S. economy, that line of thinking can be quickly dismissed as nonsense.”

Fed struggles to lower inflation to 2% target

For households carrying credit-card balances, private student loans or adjustable-rate debt, each 25-basis-point hike adds up—and analysts warn that sustained rate hikes could lift Treasury yields and keep borrowing costs elevated well into mid-2027.

“The challenge for the Fed is that we need to see 0.2% or less monthly core PCE gains consistently to return inflation to its 2% target,’’ Swonk said, describing the last nearly six years of price pressures as “the longest and most corrosive bout of inflation since the 1970s.”

“A fall in pump prices and more promotions among retailers could get us there in November – but it may not stay there,’’ Swonk said.

data.title: Oil Price Today: Brent Edges Up After Fresh Tanker Attacks Near Strait Of Hormuz
data.description:
Oil price today is edging higher after the UK's maritime security agency confirmed a tanker was hit by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran claimed two more tankers struck mines nearby.

Brent futures for February delivery, the most actively traded contract, were up $0.66, or 0.7%, at $91.30 a barrel at 16:25 UK time. That compares with Wednesday's settlement of $90.64.

US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) for January was up $1.14, or 1.4%, at $84.82.

With US markets shut for Thanksgiving, trading is thinner than usual.

What happened in Strait of Hormuz?

UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) published Warning 223-26 on Thursday, classifying the incident as an attack.

It said local authorities had reported that an outbound tanker was struck by an unknown projectile 18 nautical miles east of Khasab, Oman, at 13:00 UK time on Wednesday, November 25. The crew has been accounted for and there is no report of environmental impact.

A separate UKMTO warning said a tanker's master reported an explosion from an unknown projectile close to the vessel 50 nautical miles west of Dubai at 21:30 UK time on Wednesday. No damage was reported.

That followed Warning 221-26, which reported a tanker struck by a projectile in the strait on Sunday. UKMTO has not named any of the ships or said who fired.

What is Iran claiming?

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said two tankers "in violation of regulations" hit naval mines north of Khasab in the early hours of Thursday, according to a statement carried by Iran's Tasnim news agency.

It said one was a supertanker carrying more than 2M barrels of crude that was "left burning". The IRGC said the tankers had switched off their navigation systems and were using an unauthorised route.

Those claims have not been independently confirmed. No vessel has been named, and UKMTO had not issued a warning matching the IRGC's account by the time of writing.

Separately, Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery, causing fires.

The Saudi-led coalition said air defences destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura but did not say the refinery was hit, Al Jazeera reported.

Why is oil price not rising more?

February Brent climbed from a morning low of $89.75 at 09:20 UK time to about $91 by 11:00 UK time, after the IRGC statement was first reported.

It has not regained its day high of $92.08, touched at 05:40 UK time.

That leaves Brent well short of a 3% daily move. Traders have watched repeated attacks on Gulf shipping this month, and prices have fallen despite fresh incidents.

The two-day picture is firmer. February Brent is up 2.8% from Tuesday's settlement of $88.78.

The expiring January Brent contract, which stops trading on Monday, was at $96.00, a premium of $4.70 to February. A steep premium for the nearest month usually points to tight prompt supply.

Brent chart | Source: ICE via TradingView

What happens next for oil prices?

OPEC+ ministers meet on Sunday, November 29. The 42nd OPEC and non-OPEC Ministerial Meeting was set in June, and the seven OPEC+ countries that review output monthly also meet that day.

Any change to supply policy could matter more for prices than a single tanker incident. Production baselines for 2027 are on the agenda.

In the Gulf, the key test is whether UKMTO or the ship owners confirm the IRGC's mine claims. A confirmed hit on a fully laden supertanker would be a bigger supply story.

Thursday's low of $89.75 and high of $92.08 are the near-term levels to watch on February Brent.

Oil is caught between rising security risks in the Gulf and expectations of a supply surplus next year. That mix can trigger sharp moves in either direction, especially in thin holiday trade.

data.title: Micron And SanDisk Stocks Among The Cheapest In Tech: Should You Buy?
data.description:
Micron Technology (MU) and SanDisk (SNDK) have emerged among the most attractively valued stocks in the information technology sector, according to a recent valuation screen.

However, their low earnings multiples are raising questions about whether investors are overlooking an opportunity or anticipating a downturn in the memory industry.

The two companies have been major beneficiaries of rising demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure, as hyperscalers and technology companies invest heavily in data centres, high-bandwidth memory and storage capacity.

Yet their shares have come under pressure amid a broader sell-off in semiconductor stocks, driven by concerns that AI spending may be running ahead of the revenue and profits it can ultimately generate.

Investors are also weighing the possibility of tighter political and regulatory scrutiny of data centre construction, alongside expectations of a potential Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

Micron has fallen over 33% in the last month, while SanDisk is down over 53%.

Micron and SanDisk rank among the cheapest technology stocks

As the third-quarter earnings season draws to a close, investors are reassessing valuations across the technology sector.

Companies are experiencing different growth trajectories and margin pressures despite continued demand for AI infrastructure, semiconductors, and enterprise technology.

According to Seeking Alpha's Quant Ratings, 20 information technology stocks have attractive relative valuations.

Eight companies received an A+ Valuation Grade, the highest possible rating.

They include Arrow Electronics (ARW), Diodes (DIOD), DXC Technology (DXC), Fastly (FSLY), Micron, MaxLinear (MXL), Super Micro Computer (SMCI), and SanDisk.

The valuation discount for the two memory companies is particularly striking.

According to GuruFocus data as of November 26, SanDisk traded at 4.7 times trailing earnings, while Micron traded at 8.1 times.

Both were substantially below the sector peer median of 29.8 times.

Their forward price-to-earnings ratios were even lower, at 2.58 for SanDisk and 3.4 for Micron.

The stocks were also trading well below their respective 52-week highs, with SanDisk down 75% and Micron down 52%.

However, low multiples do not necessarily indicate that a stock is undervalued.

Memory prices are highly sensitive to changes in supply and demand, and exceptionally strong earnings can quickly deteriorate when the industry enters a weaker phase.

Why low P/E ratios may be a warning for memory stocks

The cyclical nature of the memory business is one reason investors remain cautious despite the apparent valuation opportunity.

Brendan Burke, research director for semiconductors, supply chain and emerging technology at the Futurum Group, described low price-to-earnings ratios for memory companies as a "warning label, not a bargain sign."

"Investors have learned over decades to sell memory stocks at peak earnings, because the earnings side of that ratio has historically collapsed when the cycle turns," he said in a MarketWatch report.

"A multiple in the low single digits tells you the market is pricing today's profits as a peak," he added.

However, Burke acknowledged that the current AI investment cycle may differ from previous memory booms.

The historical precedent "ignores that AI has changed the shape of this cycle."

Some types of memory, including high-bandwidth memory and solid-state-drive storage, are tied to what he called "mission-critical data-center buildouts", rather than demand for memory used in personal computers and handsets.

That distinction could make earnings "more durable than these multiples imply," Burke said.

William Blair analyst Sebastien Naji told MarketWatch that there was a limit to the usefulness of low P/E ratios as a "valuation support metric."

CreditSights analyst Andy Li also cautioned that memory stocks experience "extreme volatility in pricing", which can produce boom-and-bust cycles.

If investors continue to treat the sector as cyclical, a "dramatic price decline may well be in the cards," he said. "The price action reflects that fear."

Li explained that cyclical stocks often trade at "very low" price-to-earnings multiples near market peaks because their estimated earnings for the next 12 months are "most inflated".

They tend to bottom at relatively high multiples as earnings estimates contract.

He also pointed to the monthly options expiry on Friday as a possible technical factor influencing the stocks.

Strong AI demand faces questions over future supply

Recent financial results underline the strength of demand for memory and storage products.

Micron reported fiscal fourth-quarter 2026 revenue of $54.23 billion, compared with $11.32 billion a year earlier.

The company forecast revenue of $61.5 billion for the following quarter.

SanDisk reported $11 billion in fiscal first-quarter 2027 revenue and expects sales of between $12.2 billion and $12.6 billion in the next quarter.

The challenge for investors is determining whether these growth rates and margins can be sustained as memory producers expand capacity and more supply enters the market.

That concern has prompted some brokerages to reassess their outlook for Micron.

BNP Paribas downgraded the company to Neutral from Outperform earlier this week and cut its price target to $775 from $1,700.

The brokerage cited potential delays to data centre capacity expansion and reductions in memory content.

"Yes, Micron's shares have fallen 42% from its peak in June, but growing risks to hyperscaler capacity plans in 2028 further threaten S/D fundamentals while HBM content is being reduced in Vera Rubin Ultra, PC and mobile units will decline in ’26 and ’27, and incremental wafer capacity comes online," said BNP analyst Karl Ackerman in a Tuesday note.

"We think the downside risk to an oversupply scenario is mounting with growing risks of data center permit delays to 2028 data center capacity, content reductions in AI servers, PC, and mobile, and accelerated memory capacity by memory producers," he added.

"We think DRAM and NAND supply-demand can approach parity starting in mid-2027 and result in ASP declines, earlier than our prior view of mid-2028."

BNP now expects memory and storage costs associated with AI spending to peak at 40% in 2027 before declining to 27% by calendar year 2030.

UBS (UBS) has also scaled back its bullish outlook.

On November 25, analyst Timothy Arcuri cut his price target on Micron to $1,100 from $1,625, while retaining a Buy rating.

The contrasting signals leave investors weighing two competing possibilities: AI demand could sustain a longer and stronger memory cycle than historical patterns suggest, or current earnings could represent a cyclical peak.

For Micron and SanDisk, the sustainability of pricing and margins may ultimately matter more than how inexpensive their shares appear on conventional valuation measures.

data.title: How Spain’s Parties Plan To Raise Incomes As Low Earners Gain Ground
data.description:
Spain's monthly pay rose faster at the bottom than across much of the middle, though the largest gains were concentrated near the top. The political parties differ on how to raise incomes. Some favour a higher minimum wage and shorter working hours; others emphasise tax cuts and hiring incentives, or propose deregulation and tighter access to benefits

Between 2023 and 2025, average gross monthly pay rose by 10% in Spain’s lowest wage decile, compared with around 7% to 8% across deciles two to six. The three highest deciles recorded gains of 11% to 12%.

Over the longer period from 2019, the bottom decile recorded the strongest pay growth. Average gross monthly pay rose by about 33%, compared with 23% in the fifth decile and 27% in the top decile. Spain’s sharp minimum-wage increases are likely to have supported earnings near the bottom, although these figures cannot isolate their effect. Workers move between deciles, while changes in hours worked, occupation and seniority also affect average monthly pay.

Wage growth has been strongest at the bottom and top

Change in average gross monthly wage by overall wage decile, 2023-2025 (%)

Source: INE, ING Economic Research

Faster growth has not removed the large differences in pay. In 2025, employees in the lowest overall wage decile earned an average of €709 per month, compared with €1,970 in the fifth decile and €5,983 in the 10th.

With Spain voting on 29 November, the election programmes offer three different approaches to raising household incomes. The Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) wants to continue raising statutory wages, reduce working time and expand social support. Partido Popular places more weight on tax relief, incentives for stable employment and refundable family benefits. Vox proposes broader tax cuts, less labour regulation and tighter eligibility rules for social assistance.

Low monthly wages also reflect limited working hours

Monthly earnings depend on working time as well as wage rates. In 2025, 86.3% of employees in the lowest monthly-wage decile worked part-time. The share fell to 32.2% in the second decile and to around 9.5% and 7.5% in the third and fourth deciles, respectively. Part-time employment was uncommon from the middle of the distribution onward.

Temporary contracts followed a similar, though less extreme, pattern. They accounted for 32.7% of employees in the first decile and 18.9% in the second, compared with 3.9% in the top decile. Employees with a foreign nationality represented more than one-fifth of the first three deciles: 20.9%, 24.5%, and 25.0%, respectively.

Part-time and temporary work are concentrated in lower wage deciles

Share of employees in each overall wage decile, 2025 (%)

Source: INE, ING Economic Research

These figures put the minimum wage debate into perspective. A higher wage floor can raise hourly or full-time-equivalent pay, but it cannot guarantee enough paid hours. Someone working a short or irregular schedule can remain on a low monthly income even when the statutory rate rises. Contract stability, predictable schedules and access to full-time work therefore matter alongside the wage floor.

The programmes rely on different combinations of wage regulation, working-time rules, tax reductions, cash benefits and public services.

PSOE would continue the wage-led approach

PSOE would continue using the minimum wage as part of a broader labour market strategy. Since 2018, the monthly rate has risen from €736 to €1,221, paid 14 times a year. The programme would place the minimum wage above 60% of the average wage in law, with future adjustments reflecting prices, wages, productivity and workers’ needs.

Spain has already moved substantially towards a higher wage floor. The minimum wage rose from 41.0% of the median full-time wage in 2018 to 55.3% in 2025, an increase of more than 14 percentage points. France remained above 60%, while Germany and the Netherlands recorded much smaller increases.

Spain’s minimum wage has moved much closer to the median wage

Statutory minimum wage as a percentage of the median full-time wage

Source: OECD, ING Economic Research

The chart above uses the median full-time wage, while PSOE’s proposed legal benchmark refers to the average wage, so the measures are not directly comparable. Both show that further increases would start from a much higher relative level than in 2018. Low-paid employees have recorded the strongest wage growth while employment has continued to rise, but additional increases may be harder for businesses with low productivity or narrow margins.

PSOE would also reduce the standard working week to 37.5 hours without loss of pay and encourage collective bargaining towards 35 hours. Transitional arrangements would support smaller companies, but the combination of higher wages and shorter hours would still raise hourly labour costs. Firms would need to respond through higher productivity, lower margins, higher prices or changes in employment and hours.

The party also wants employers to justify why positions are not offered on a full-time basis and would treat contracts covering more than 80% of a standard schedule as full-time. This targets an important source of low monthly earnings: insufficient paid hours.

Beyond the labour market, PSOE proposes more support for lower-income families through a progressive child benefit, a refundable child tax credit and wider access to childcare and care services. These measures could reach households that receive little from conventional tax allowances, but would also create permanent fiscal costs.

Partido Popular would focus more on disposable income

Partido Popular focuses less on statutory wage targets or shorter working hours and more on tax cuts, incentives for stable employment and support for families.

The party proposes lower personal income tax rates for low and middle-income households, higher personal and family allowances, and an automatic income tax exemption for anyone earning the minimum wage. Tax thresholds would again be adjusted for inflation. Workers and self-employed people aged 18 to 35 would receive a four-year tax reduction, beginning with a full exemption in the first year and declining thereafter.

Tax reductions can increase take-home pay without adding directly to employers’ wage bills. They may therefore carry less immediate employment risk than another large increase in the wage floor. Their reach is weaker at the bottom, however. Workers whose earnings already fall below the income-tax threshold gain little from a conventional tax cut. This includes many people with short working hours.

Partido Popular partly addresses this through refundable family support. Existing deductions would be combined into a monthly payment available even when a household’s tax liability was too low to use the full deduction. The programme also proposes free education from birth to age three, more flexible arrangements for caregivers and a deduction covering 40% of professional care expenses for an elderly dependent relative.

Employers would pay lower unemployment contributions when the stability of their workforce exceeded the average in their sector. New self-employed workers would pay no social security contributions during their first year, with a possible second year for those earning below the minimum wage.

The distributional effect would depend on the balance between conventional tax relief, which offers less to people with little taxable income, and refundable support that can reach poorer households.

Vox would cut taxes and narrow access to benefits

Vox also relies heavily on lower taxation. It proposes a simpler personal income tax system, with rates adjusted for the number of children. Self-employed workers earning below the minimum wage would pay no social security contributions, with contributions rising progressively above that threshold.

Vox would repeal the current government’s labour legislation, which it argues has failed to eliminate insecure employment. The programme promises stable jobs and higher wages, but provides little detail on the rules that would replace the existing framework or how wages would increase.

The party also proposes free education from birth to age three, childcare support and stronger care services. Access would be more restrictive, however. Spanish nationals would receive priority for housing and various social benefits, and the minimum-income scheme would be limited to them.

Foreign nationals are disproportionately represented in the lower wage deciles. These restrictions would therefore reduce support for a group with relatively high exposure to low pay, temporary employment and housing pressure.

The choice concerns instruments, recipients and financing

Gross wages are only one part of household living standards. Tax cuts can raise net earnings but offer little to people with low taxable income, while refundable benefits and public services can reach those households more directly.

The programmes follow a clear left-right divide. PSOE relies on wage regulation, shorter hours, employment protection and public provision. Partido Popular emphasises tax relief, refundable family support and employer incentives. Vox combines broader tax cuts and less labour market regulation with tighter access to benefits.

Ahead of the election on 29 November, most polls point to a parliamentary majority for Partido Popular and Vox. If that produces a government, policy would probably shift towards tax relief, employer incentives and greater labour-market flexibility. The extent of the change would depend on the seat distribution and Vox’s influence.

Spain has shown that strong wage growth at the bottom can coexist with rising employment. Repeating that performance may be harder from today’s higher wage floor, especially when many low-paid employees lack access to sufficient working hours or stable contracts. Higher wage floors and shorter working weeks carry risks for low-productivity employers, while conventional tax cuts often miss the lowest earners. The challenge for the next government will be to raise disposable incomes without weakening employment or creating unsustainable fiscal commitments.

data.title: Thanksgiving Inflation, The Fed’s Debt Trap, And Gold’s Eastward Shift
data.description:
In the latest Money Metals Midweek Memo, host Mike Maharrey connects the rising cost of Thanksgiving dinner to a larger problem facing the U.S. economy: persistent inflation, record debt, and a Federal Reserve caught between fighting rising prices and keeping a debt-heavy economy afloat.

Maharrey also examines the recent sell-off in gold and silver, the scramble for liquidity on Wall Street, and surging Chinese gold demand. His central argument is that short-term pressure on precious metals has not erased gold’s long-term case.

Thanksgiving Dinner Costs Rise 6% in 2026

A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people is expected to cost an average of $58.63 this year, about 6% more than in 2025, according to the Farm Bureau. The organization has tracked grocery prices for 40 years, using hundreds of volunteers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico.

That increase is nearly double the roughly 3.5% inflation rate measured by the Consumer Price Index, Maharrey noted. It also ends a three-year trend of falling Thanksgiving meal costs.

The longer-term comparison looks different. Since 2012, the cost of a traditional Thanksgiving dinner has risen about 18.5%, while cumulative CPI inflation has reached roughly 49%. Since October 2021, food prices in the CPI’s “food at home” index have climbed 22%, compared with an increase of about 10% for the traditional Thanksgiving meal.

Maharrey said the difference reflects how inflation moves unevenly across the economy. Supply and demand affect individual prices, while grocery stores may discount turkey and other holiday staples to bring customers in. Those changing prices can coexist with a general rise in the overall price level.

Inflation Compounds Even When It Cools

Maharrey cautioned that slower inflation does not mean prices are falling. It means they are rising at a slower pace. Even the Federal Reserve’s 2% inflation target compounds over time, steadily reducing the purchasing power of money.

Inflation, Maharrey argued, has remained above 2% for 68 consecutive months. He questioned whether policymakers can bring it down to target without damaging an economy weighed down by government, corporate, and consumer debt.

The debate has become central to the outlook for gold and silver. Maharrey said market commentary has focused on expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December and keep rates higher for longer. He argued that this view often overlooks the strain higher borrowing costs place on an already indebted economy.

The Federal Reserve’s Inflation and Debt Dilemma

The episode framed the policy debate as a Fed “catch-22.” Higher interest rates may help restrain inflation, but they also make it more expensive to service debt and can put pressure on businesses and consumers.

Maharrey cited U.S. national debt above $40.5 trillion, with the total approaching $40.7 trillion and potentially reaching $41 trillion within the next month or two. He also pointed to more than $1 trillion in annual federal interest expense, rising small-business bankruptcies, and consumers struggling with high-interest credit card debt.

Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman has warned that continued rate hikes could push the United States into recession. In a post on X, Ackman called further increases another mistake and said financial conditions had already tightened sharply. Maharrey cited SpaceX securing debt financing at 8.25%, compared with a 6% rate on its unsecured bond offering at the time of its IPO in June.

Maharrey also cited small-business bankruptcies rising 46% during the first nine months of 2026 and an increase in delinquent auto loans as signs of financial strain. In his view, rate hikes could intensify pressure across an economy carrying heavy debt loads.

Ackman has argued that a 3% inflation target may be more realistic in a world shaped by geopolitical risk, military spending, tariffs, deglobalization, and investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and energy. Maharrey challenged the idea that a higher target solves inflation, arguing that it would instead accept a faster loss of purchasing power.

Years of Easy Money Complicate the Fed’s Choices

Maharrey traced the current dilemma to years of monetary stimulus. After the 2008 financial crisis, the Federal Reserve held rates near zero for almost a decade. A limited attempt to normalize rates in 2018 was followed by rate cuts and renewed quantitative easing.

By the time the COVID-19 pandemic began, the Fed had already cut rates three times and expanded its balance sheet. During the pandemic, it brought rates back to zero and injected nearly $5 trillion into the economy through quantitative easing.

When the Fed began raising rates in March 2022, the change helped trigger a banking crisis, Maharrey said. He argued that this history shows how difficult it may be to withdraw monetary support without causing significant economic stress.

Maharrey believes that, when forced to choose between fighting inflation and supporting the economy during a crisis, the Federal Reserve has historically chosen stimulus. He expects the central bank could eventually cut rates and expand money creation again, even if that means renewed inflationary pressure.

Why Gold and Silver Have Fallen

Gold was trading below $3,500 an ounce as Maharrey recorded the episode, nearly $2,000 below its January high. He described himself as short-term bearish on precious metals, while maintaining that the growing debt burden supports gold’s longer-term outlook.

One factor behind the sell-off, he said, is a scramble for liquidity. As investors sell assets to raise cash, gold and silver can fall alongside stocks, even though precious metals are often viewed as safe havens. Investors may sell highly liquid gold to cover margin calls or exit losing trades.

Maharrey pointed to similar behavior during the early stages of the 2008 financial crisis and the pandemic. In his view, gold’s initial decline during market stress does not necessarily signal that its safe-haven role has disappeared.

Chinese Gold Demand Surges as Western Investors Sell

While Western investors have been selling, Chinese buyers have continued accumulating gold. China imported 155.9 metric tons in October, up 174% from October 2025. The value of China’s gold imports reached a record $29 billion so far in 2026, and gold was the country’s third-largest import category in October.

Gold withdrawals from the Shanghai Gold Exchange also strengthened during a month when they typically ease. Withdrawals rose 2% month over month to 94 tons in October, according to the World Gold Council. Maharrey said dip buying and strong bullion sales helped drive the increase.

He also noted speculation that higher gold imports could help reduce the appearance of China’s large trade surplus by increasing the value of imports. More broadly, he described a pattern in which price weakness in Western markets has coincided with continued gold accumulation in China and India.

Trading-hour data cited in the episode showed gold rising 12.9% during Asian trading hours in the first six months of the year, while falling 15% during North American trading hours. Gold declined 1.3% during European hours over the same period. Maharrey said the pattern points to a shift in gold flows from Western markets toward Asia, where new infrastructure is also being developed to challenge Western dominance in gold trading.

Maharrey’s Outlook: Short-Term Volatility, Long-Term Inflation Risk

Maharrey’s outlook combines caution about the near term with a bullish long-term view of gold. Precious metals may remain under pressure as investors seek liquidity and markets respond to interest-rate expectations. But he argues that heavy debt, the limits of monetary tightening, and the possibility of renewed stimulus continue to support gold’s long-term role as an inflation hedge.

As the holiday season begins, Maharrey also highlighted gold and silver as potential gifts, describing them as tangible assets that can be held over time. He directed listeners to Money Metals for precious metals products, market news, and information about buying, selling, and storing bullion.
